The [2018 Data Science Bowl](https://www.kaggle.com/c/data-science-bowl-2018) asked for the
nuclei in microscopy images: several hundred pictures, taken down different microscopes under
different stains, each with its nuclei outlined. It is a good first problem because it is
genuinely varied and genuinely small.

This walks through it end to end.

**Where the numbers come from.** The figure and the foreground shares below were produced on
this machine by the code shown; the trained rows are
[`examples/data_science_bowl.yaml`](https://github.com/maju116/pyplatypus/blob/main/examples/data_science_bowl.yaml)'s,
and the published weights' scores are the registry's own. Nothing was trained to write this
page.

## Before any of that: a mask in four lines

A model trained on this data is published, so the shortest way to see whether the package
does anything useful is to borrow it. No training, no waiting:

```python
import pyplatypus as pp

published = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "semantic_segmentation",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "validation_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "mode": "nested_dirs",
            "colormap": [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]],
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "nuclei",
                "input_shape": [256, 256],
                "weights": "dsbowl-unet",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
engine = pp.build_engine(published)
engine.fit()
masks = engine.predict("nuclei", "validation")
masks.shape
```

**`fit()` is still the call and `fit: false` only changes what it does** - with the flag set
it loads rather than trains. `build_engine` reads the data and builds the model; a `predict`
straight after it answers *no model has been trained or loaded yet*.

Notice what the specification does **not** say: no `architecture`, no `blocks`, no `filters`.
A published file records its own geometry and the engine adopts it, so naming them would risk
a specification that disagrees with the file - and the file would win.

```python
figure = pp.plot_masks(images, prediction=masks[:3])
```

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maju116/pyplatypus/main/assets/article-dsbowl-published.png)

The weights came down from the Hub on first use and are cached afterwards, so running this
again costs nothing. `tools/readme_figures.py article-dsbowl` is the script that drew it.

**No score is reported here, on purpose.** This directory and the one the weights were trained
on come from the same collection and overlap, so anything measured here would flatter the
model. The numbers that mean something were measured on a held-out split when the weights were
published, and travel with them - `available_weights()` carries the description, and it says
these are *semantic*, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them
would be wrong. [Telling touching nuclei apart](instances.qmd) is the article about that.

One thing worth meeting here rather than later. **Weights belong to an exact model, not to a
task**, and the rest of this page trains at 160x160 while these were trained at 256:

```python
mismatched = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "semantic_segmentation",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "validation_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "mode": "nested_dirs",
            "colormap": [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]],
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "nuclei",
                "architecture": "u_net",
                "input_shape": [160, 160],
                "blocks": 4,
                "filters": 16,
                "weights": "dsbowl-unet",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
pp.build_engine(mismatched).fit()
```

```
WeightsError: 'dsbowl-unet' was trained for a different model:
  - input_shape: weights say (256, 256), the model says (160, 160)
Loading anyway would either fail inside torch or, where the shapes happen to agree, produce
a model that predicts confidently and means nothing.
```

**The file itself is fine and that is the point of the two stages.** `from_dict` accepts
this: every field is spelled correctly and `160` is a legal `input_shape`. The refusal comes
when the weights are loaded, because only then is there something to compare them against -
which is why the message names the field rather than a tensor size.

Refused with the field that differs, and before torch was reached. That check exists because
the failure it prevents is silent: weights trained on a different colormap with the same
number of classes load perfectly and predict nonsense.

Everything below trains a model from scratch instead, which is what you will actually do on
your own data - the published weights are a demonstration and a baseline, not an answer to
your problem.

## The data

One directory per image, each holding an `images` and a `masks` subdirectory. The masks
subdirectory holds **one file per nucleus**:

```
stage1_train/
  00ae65c1c.../
    images/00ae65c1c....png
    masks/8a0ac8e3c....png      # one file per nucleus, 27 of them in this case
    masks/9a1e2f4b7....png
    ...
```

536 cases in `stage1_train` and 134 in `stage1_validation`, and `mode: nested_dirs` is what
reads that shape. For a semantic task the per-nucleus files are united - their element-wise
maximum - which is the step that turns *which nucleus* into *nucleus or not*. That is the
right thing here and the wrong thing for counting, which is the other article's subject.

## Look at it before training on it

The most useful thing to know before choosing anything else is how much of each picture is
actually the thing you are looking for.

```python
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

def foreground(case: Path, size=(160, 160)) -> float:
    united = np.zeros(size, dtype=bool)
    for file in (case / "masks").glob("*.png"):
        united |= pp.read_image(file, channels=1, size=size, nearest=True)[..., 0] > 0.5
    return float(united.mean())
```

Over forty cases drawn from `stage1_validation`, measured on this machine:

| | min | Q1 | median | mean | Q3 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| foreground share | 0.013 | 0.033 | 0.109 | 0.133 | 0.214 | 0.455 |

Nuclei are a minority of the pixels in every image, and how small a minority **varies by a
factor of 35** between images. Both facts are worth acting on now rather than discovering
later. The R vignette this page mirrors reports 0.011 to 0.334 over its own forty - a
different sample of the same data, and the same conclusion.

Because the foreground is a minority, a model that predicts background everywhere and finds
nothing at all still scores well on accuracy, and well on a Dice averaged over both classes.
So the metrics in the configuration below are asked for with `include_background: false`: the
number reported is then the one about the nuclei, and a model that finds none of them scores
zero, as it should.

Because the share varies so much, the loss has to hold up at both ends. Plain cross-entropy
will happily settle into predicting background on the sparse images; blending it with Dice, or
using Focal-Tversky with `alpha` above a half, keeps the rare class worth getting right.

## The specification

Two models, so there is something to compare. They share the data and differ in architecture
and objective - `u_net` with `cce_dice`, and `linknet` with `focal_tversky` at `alpha: 0.7`:

```yaml
models:
  - name: unet
    architecture: u_net
    input_shape: [160, 160]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    loss:
      name: cce_dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
      - name: iou
        include_background: false
    epochs: 6

  - name: linknet
    architecture: linknet
    input_shape: [160, 160]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    loss:
      name: focal_tversky
      alpha: 0.7            # weight missed nuclei more than false alarms
    epochs: 6
```

The `alpha: 0.7` weights false negatives above false positives: it would rather flag something
that is not a nucleus than miss one. Whether that is the right trade depends entirely on what
the count is for.

## Train

```python
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec, num_workers=4)
history = engine.fit(verbose=True)
```

`num_workers=4` is worth copying: the GPU spends most of a run waiting for PNGs to be decoded,
and nothing about the model changes.

## Compare

`engine.evaluate("validation")` returns one row per model, and the columns to read are the
metrics rather than the loss.

**Read the `loss` column with care, and note that `loss_function` sits beside it.** These two
models were trained on different objectives, so their losses are not on a common scale - a
Focal-Tversky of 0.31 is not better or worse than a CCE-Dice of 0.22, it is not the same
question. The metrics are comparable, because they measure the mask rather than the objective.

That is the column this table exists to make unquotable, and it is the same shape of mistake
as `dice` in the instance table, where a mean over a different number of class channels made
two models look 0.09 apart when their masks were 0.006 apart.

## Look at what it did

```python
predictions = engine.predict("unet", "validation")
figure = pp.plot_masks(images, prediction=predictions[shown], truth=truth)
```

The last column is the one that repays attention. Green is what was found, red what was
missed, yellow what was invented - and a single overlap score cannot tell you which of the
three you have.

On this data almost all of the red is a thin rim around nuclei that were otherwise found. The
model is locating nuclei well and drawing them slightly too small. If the question is *how
many nuclei are there*, that hardly matters. If it is *how large are they*, it is exactly what
matters - and the fix is a longer run or a loss that weights boundaries, not a different
architecture.

Neither the Dice nor any other single number distinguishes those two situations from a model
that found three quarters of the nuclei and missed the rest. That is the reason to draw the
picture.

## The same thing from a file

Everything above is one file in this repository:

```python
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl.yaml")
```

The configuration guide walks the fields; [Every configuration field](config.qmd) is the
reference beside it, generated from the models that read the file.

## A note on older graphics cards

PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta
generations - a GTX 10-series card cannot run them, and no driver update changes that.

This package does not install torch and will not choose a build for you. You install your own,
so the equivalent of the R package's `platypus_use_torch("pascal")` is asking your index for
the CUDA 12 wheels. If `torch.cuda.is_available()` is `False` on a machine that has a GPU,
that is the first thing to check - otherwise everything above runs on the processor instead,
perhaps ten times slower, and says nothing about it.
